docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The words you need before your first scorecard. Everything else is explained on the page that uses it.

Term Meaning Case One eval question, written in YAML: the input, the rubrics a right answer meets, and the checks to run. Dataset A directory of cases, run and tracked together. The directory name is the dataset name, and subfolders become tags you can run alone. Sync Copying a dataset directory to the server. Runs do it for you. Workspace Where datasets, agents and experiments live: your own (named after you), or a shared one such as dev. Every user can read every workspace; only the owner changes a personal one, and admins and writers change a shared one. Reference name@workspace, for example acme@dev. A bare name means your own workspace. Agent Your agent, registered once on the server. A code-driven agent is run by your own code; this is the usual way to start. Task The function run_experiment calls once per case. It calls your agent and returns the answer. Experiment One run of a dataset against an agent. Run One case answered once. Trace, span, session What your agent records as it works: one span per model call or tool call. One run is one session. Mapping Which span attribute holds the model, the messages, the tokens and each tool call. Trajectory The step-by-step record of a run that evalkit builds from the spans. Judge The LLM that grades an answer against the case's rubrics. Evaluator One scoring check, for example the rubric check or "did the agent call this tool". Scorecard The table of scores for an experiment, per case and per bucket (content, trajectory, presentation, efficiency, custom). Unreviewed A case in a shared dataset with no review decision at its current content. It runs like any other case; review decides promotion. Promotion An admin links a shared workspace to a target (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod). Approving a case in dev adds it, approved, to the same-named dataset in prod. Datasets in prod are fed only that way. evalkit.yaml The file in your repo that says where your cases are and which environment variables hold API keys.

Next: Try locally to see these on a running server, or the Quickstart to connect your own agent.

docs.title: Config: evalkit.yaml
docs.text:
evalkit.yaml sits at the root of the repository that holds your eval cases or your agent. The CLI and the SDK look for it above the current directory. It names the case and fixture directories and the API keys the runs from this machine use.

cases: eval/cases # optional: directory whose children are datasets
fixtures: eval/fixtures # optional: fixture bytes, flat, keyed by filename

credentials: # values are env:NAME, read when a run needs them
  agents:
    myagent: env:MYAGENT_KEY # a bare name means your own workspace
  evaluators:
    citation_check: env:EVALUATOR_KEY
  llm_providers:
    https://litellm.example.com: env:LITELLM_API_KEY # keyed by the judge's base URL

Only your personal Harness API agents use credentials.agents here. The server drives shared agents (ouragent@dev) with the keys stored in its database, so an entry for one in evalkit.yaml is never read. The same holds for shared remote evaluators.

Put the values in a .env file next to evalkit.yaml (and keep it out of git), or in your shell. A variable set in the shell wins over .env.

Agents, remote evaluators and the judge are not configured here:

  • Agents are created once on the server with evalkit agents create (or on the Agents page). A personal agent runs from your machine; a shared one is driven by the server. An agent without a harness URL is code-driven: only run_experiment can run it. See SDK runs.
  • Remote evaluators are created with evalkit evaluators create. A run uses the evaluators in its agent's workspace.
  • The judge of an experiment is the server's default judge (an admin sets it with evalkit judge-default set) unless you pick one: evalkit run … --judge-model M --judge-base-url URL --judge-effort E, the run dialog's "Judge provider" picker, or run_experiment(judge=Judge(...)). Re-evaluating an experiment always reuses its judge.

Rules:

  • env:NAME values are read only when a command needs them. A missing variable is an error that names it.
  • An agent or evaluator with no credentials entry is called without a key, and the run prints one line saying so. A judge with no entry stops the run before its first case: no credentials.llm_providers entry for <url>.
  • credentials.judges is now credentials.llm_providers. A file that still uses the old name fails to load.
  • An llm_providers key may itself be env:NAME (env:LLM_BASE_URL: env:LLM_API_KEY), so the judge's base URL can come from the environment too. A key whose variable is unset is skipped.
  • cases and fixtures are optional. Leave them out when you only run shared datasets, for example from run_experiment. Commands that need them say so:
  • evalkit sync <name> and evalkit run <name> on a dataset in your workspace need cases to find <cases>/<name>. Passing the dataset's directory instead (evalkit sync eval/cases/finance) works without it.
  • A sync uploads fixture bytes from fixtures. Without it, a case whose fixture the server does not already hold fails the sync with E-FIXTURE-MISSING.
  • run_experiment on a dataset in your workspace skips the sync without cases and runs the copy the server holds.
  • Fixtures a run downloads go to fixtures, or to a temporary directory when it is not set.

docs.title: Harness API
docs.text:
The Harness API is the HTTP contract a client's agent harness implements so evalkit can drive it: start a run, poll its status, serve its trajectory. Agents in a shared workspace are driven by this server; agents in a personal workspace by evalkit run from their owner's machine. The OpenAPI schema ships inside the CLI:

evalkit contracts export --target ./contracts   # harness-api-v1.json, atif-accepted.json, …

Each endpoint lets evalkit do one thing. Every Harness API has the first three; declare the rest in the capabilities response when you implement them. An agent on the SDK + traces path has no Harness API and none of these endpoints; evalkit sees what its task returns and the spans it exports.

Endpoint Lets evalkit Capability flag Without it GET /capabilities see what the harness supports and gate evaluators on it (snapshotted per experiment) part of every Harness API — POST /runs invoke the agent: start one run in a fresh session with the case input and files part of every Harness API — GET /runs/{id} wait for the run and read its answer, structured output, model and artifact list part of every Harness API — GET /runs/{id}/trajectory read the trajectory (ATIF): the run view, trajectory evaluators and token/cost gauges provides.trajectory trajectory evaluators skip, unless the agent's trajectory source is otel and the trajectory comes from spans GET /runs/{id}/files, GET /runs/{id}/files/{path} read the workspace: the run's Workspace tab, downloads and artifact copies provides.workspace no Workspace tab; artifacts the run reports are not copied GET /runs list the agent's sessions on the Runs page and for evalkit runs list/runs pull, including ones evalkit did not start; optional since/until filter by creation time provides.run_listing the Runs page is empty for this agent POST /runs/{id}/stop cancel a run that hit its time limit accepts.stop timed-out runs keep running on the harness

POST /runs takes JSON, or multipart when the case has fixture files and the harness accepts files but not file_urls. Run status moves through queued, running, then one of completed, failed, cancelled.

A code-driven agent (no harness_url) has none of these endpoints, so its runs have no Workspace tab. To see an agent's files in evalkit, give it a Harness API with at least the files endpoints; its trajectory can still come from traces.

Every request carries x-api-key. Two rules matter more than the rest:

  • Capabilities honesty. Declare only what works. evalkit neutral-skips evaluators whose inputs the harness does not provide; a false true produces failing scores blamed on the agent.
  • Implement stop. evalkit calls stop on timeout when accepts.stop is true; a harness without it leaks resources on every timed-out run.

docs.title: Already have a harness? Keep it
docs.text:
A harness that already emits OpenTelemetry traces can skip the trajectory endpoint: create the agent with --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE and export spans to the collector with the run id it returned from POST /runs in the attribute the mapping's session_id rule names (session.id for OpenInference, gen_ai.conversation.id for GenAI). Everything else stays: server runs, evalkit run, the Workspace tab. The harness declares provides.trajectory: false. See Tracing.

The session evalkit polls is the run_id that POST /runs returns; there is no separate session field. A queue-backed agent whose worker opens its own session can return that session id as run_id, or stamp the run_id it returned on the job's spans in the mapping's session id attribute. Either way the ids must also work with the other /runs/{id} endpoints.

Moving to SDK runs instead only makes sense to stop hosting the harness. A code-driven agent loses server-started runs and the Workspace tab, and run_experiment refuses an agent with a harness_url: keep one agent name and run it with evalkit run, rather than adding a second entry for run_experiment.

docs.title: Checking
docs.text:
evalkit harness check ouragent@dev

runs a trivial call, exercises every declared capability and prints a pass/fail table. For a harness agent whose trajectory source is otel the trajectory row reads "from traces" and a session row reports the collected spans.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
evalkit is one Python package on PyPI, evalkit-py. It holds the evalkit command (the CLI), the evalkit.sdk module for SDK runs and, with the server extra, the server itself.

Your CLI and SDK must run the same version as the evalkit server you use: local runs and SDK runs refuse to start otherwise. The commands on this page pin version 0.3.0. On your server's own /docs/install page, that is the server's version; curl <server url>/api/cli prints it anywhere.

docs.title: The CLI, as a global tool
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.3.0"

With pipx instead: pipx install --force "evalkit-py==0.3.0".

curl http://localhost:8020/api/cli prints the server's version, for scripts and CI:

uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==$(curl -fsSL http://localhost:8020/api/cli | jq -r .version)"

docs.title: The SDK, into a project
docs.text:
run_experiment and tracing.register live in the same package as the CLI. The otel extra brings the OpenTelemetry SDK and the OTLP exporter. Pin the server's version; uv.lock records it:

uv add "evalkit-py[otel]==0.3.0"

With pip instead: pip install "evalkit-py[otel]==0.3.0".

To keep evalkit out of the app's dependencies, run the eval script with it instead:

uv run --with "evalkit-py[otel]==0.3.0" python eval/run.py

docs.title: The server
docs.text:
pip install "evalkit-py[server]" installs the server too: the API, the web UI and migrations. To run one on your machine against a Postgres you already have:

evalkit init-server   # creates the database, writes config.yaml and .env in ./evalkit-try
cd evalkit-try && evalkit serve

Try locally walks through it with a sample agent; the evalkit-deployment skill covers running a server for a team.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Every API response carries X-Evalkit-Version. The CLI warns when it differs from the server and refuses when the major versions differ. Local runs and SDK runs refuse any difference, so after a server deploy, from the project's root:

evalkit update

It reinstalls the CLI at the server's version and, when pyproject.toml pins evalkit-py==…, moves the pin and runs uv sync. It then refreshes the skills in every directory evalkit skills install wrote to on this machine (listed in ~/.evalkit/skills-targets), and in ./.claude/skills or ./.agents/skills if they hold an earlier install; commit the changes in repos that track the skills. Pass --no-skills to skip that.

A project that vendored an evalkit wheel before evalkit was on PyPI moves to PyPI once: uv remove evalkit && uv add "evalkit-py[otel]==0.3.0".

Next: Login.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020

The command asks for your username and password and stores the server URL and your token in ~/.evalkit/config.toml. The CLI talks to one server at a time: logging in again, to the same server or another, replaces the stored login. Dev and prod are workspaces on one server (finance@dev, finance@prod), not separate logins.

Tokens expire after the TTL the deployer configured (30 days by default). evalkit whoami shows who the token logs in as and when it expires, and exits 1 if the server rejects it; run it before a long run. Commands that talk to the server warn when the token expires within a day. When commands start failing with 401, log in again.

docs.title: Scripts and CI
docs.text:
Two environment variables bypass the config file:

export EVALKIT_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:8020
export EVALKIT_TOKEN=<token>

A stored token expires, so CI jobs should log in at the start of every run with a password from the secret store:

evalkit login --url "$EVALKIT_SERVER_URL" --username admin --password "$EVALKIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD"

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
The CLI and the SDK wait up to 120 seconds for each server call. Set EVALKIT_TIMEOUT (seconds) to wait longer, for example on a slow network:

export EVALKIT_TIMEOUT=300

It covers calls to the evalkit server only. The server's own calls to an agent's harness keep their fixed limits, and so does evalkit harness check.

The SDK uses the same login and the same two variables. A deployed agent that only exports traces uses an agent token instead; see Tracing.

docs.title: Mappings
docs.text:
A mapping tells evalkit which span attribute holds each field of the evalkit span format (ESF): the span kind, the session id, the model, the messages, the token counts, the tool name and call id. It also says where the run's answer comes from (answer) and which spans to leave out (exclude_spans).

Every agent whose trajectories come from traces has its own mapping. evalkit agents create NAME --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE makes the first version active. Start from the connect-traces skill's openinference.json or gen_ai.json, which cover agents on the OpenInference or GenAI semantic conventions as they are. Spans that reach an agent with no active mapping are stored without a session id.

An existing agent switches between ATIF and traces with evalkit agents edit NAME --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE (or --trajectory-source atif), or from the agent's Edit dialog. Switching to traces without a file reuses the agent's last active mapping. The switch is refused while one of the agent's experiments is running, and experiments that already ran keep the source they ran with.

A mapping applies to every span of the agent and is versioned: evalkit traces mapping push creates a draft, you review the draft against recent sessions on the agent's Mappings tab (Agents → the agent → Mappings), and activate it there. The connect-traces skill walks a coding agent through writing one.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
{
  "schema_version": "1",
  "kind": {
    "attribute": "openinference.span.kind",
    "values": {
      "LLM": "llm",
      "TOOL": "tool",
      "AGENT": "agent",
      "CHAIN": "chain",
      "RETRIEVER": "retriever"
    }
  },
  "session_id": {
    "attribute": "session.id"
  },
  "model": {
    "attribute": "llm.model_name"
  },
  "input_messages": {
    "attribute": "llm.input_messages",
    "message_format": "openinference"
  },
  "output_messages": {
    "attribute": "llm.output_messages",
    "message_format": "openinference"
  },
  "tokens": {
    "prompt": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt"
    },
    "completion": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.completion"
    },
    "cached": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read"
    },
    "cache_write": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_write"
    }
  },
  "cost_usd": {
    "attribute": "llm.cost.total"
  },
  "tool": {
    "name": {
      "attribute": "tool.name"
    },
    "call_id": {
      "attribute": "tool.id"
    },
    "arguments": {
      "attribute": "input.value",
      "json": true
    },
    "result": {
      "attribute": "output.value"
    }
  },
  "agent_name": {
    "attribute": "agent.name"
  },
  "input": {
    "attribute": "input.value",
    "json": true
  },
  "output": {
    "attribute": "output.value",
    "json": true
  },
  "known_attributes": [
    "openinference.span.kind",
    "session.id",
    "user.id",
    "metadata",
    "tag.tags",
    "input.mime_type",
    "output.mime_type",
    "llm.provider",
    "llm.system",
    "llm.invocation_parameters",
    "llm.finish_reason",
    "llm.tools.*",
    "llm.token_count.total",
    "llm.token_count.prompt_details.*",
    "llm.token_count.completion_details.*",
    "llm.cost.*",
    "tool.description",
    "tool.parameters",
    "tool.json_schema",
    "agent.name",
    "graph.node.*"
  ]
}

That is the skill's openinference.json. Its gen_ai.json reads gen_ai.operation.name (chat, execute_tool, invoke_agent, …), gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.input.messages / gen_ai.output.messages with "message_format": "gen_ai", gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and friends, reads the system prompt from gen_ai.system_instructions, cache writes from gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens and the agent's name from gen_ai.agent.name, and sets "cost_usd": null because the conventions define no cost attribute. Both list the other attributes of their convention under known_attributes, so evalkit traces check does not report them as unmapped; entries may be exact keys or globs such as llm.tools.*.

Rule shapes:

Shape Result {"attribute": K} the attribute's value, or null {"attribute": K, "json": true} the value parsed as JSON when it is a string; the string stays when parsing fails {"attribute": K, "values": {...}} the value translated through the table; an unlisted kind becomes other {"attribute": K, "message_format": F} the messages laid out under K per format F: openinference (flattened indexed keys), gen_ai (JSON list of messages with parts), openai (JSON list of chat messages) null never read

Two more fields shape the trajectory: answer (root, a span name, or <span name>.<output key>; default root) and exclude_spans (span names left out; default none).

Every mapping is complete on its own; there is no inheritance. The schema ships as span-mapping-v1.json with evalkit contracts export.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --dump spans.json   # read the raw attributes
evalkit traces mapping push myagent eval/span-mapping.json    # upload a draft
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --mapping draft     # preview with the draft
evalkit traces mapping list myagent

Repeat until the unmapped list holds nothing that matters and the counts look right, then activate the draft on the agent's Mappings tab. --activate on push activates in the same step; a coding agent passes it only when the developer has approved the document.

Runs record the mapping version they were converted with; a later mapping change never alters a scored run. The Runs page converts sessions on demand with the active mapping.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: The server is also an MCP server at http://localhost:8020/mcp (streamable HTTP). An agent connected to it can read every agent's runs and trajectories, and every experiment's scores. It cannot change anything.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
With an evalkit login token (evalkit login stores it in ~/.evalkit/config.toml):

claude mcp add --transport http evalkit http://localhost:8020/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $EVALKIT_TOKEN"

Only login tokens work here: agent tokens (evalkit tokens create) and download tickets are refused.

When the server's config has an mcp.oauth block, MCP clients that speak OAuth (Claude, Cursor, Codex) can connect with the URL alone: the server points them to the identity provider, and a token issued for http://localhost:8020/mcp with the configured scope (mcp.oauth.scope, default evalkit:read) is accepted. Evalkit login tokens keep working next to it.

mcp:
  oauth:
    issuer: https://id.example.com
    jwks_uri: https://id.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
    # audience: defaults to <server.base_url>/mcp
    # scope: your identity provider's name for read access; defaults to evalkit:read

An OAuth token is not an evalkit user. Whoever the identity provider gives that scope reads everything an evalkit login reads, which today is every workspace, and archiving someone in evalkit does not cut off their OAuth access: revoke it at the identity provider.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it returns find_agents Agents and the id (name@workspace) the run tools take find_runs An agent's runs in a time window, newest first: id, title, time, user_id, client_id, app or eval. include adds each run's metrics, turns or tool_calls (what it called, with which arguments). failed_only keeps runs with a failure; tool_error keeps runs where that tool errored. timezone reads date-only bounds as get_run_stats does. Up to 5,000 rows when listing alone, 200 with include or a filter get_runs Up to 200 runs by id: turns, failed turns, failures, duration, cost and where it came from, tokens, cost by model, tool errors by tool, opening question, final answer; include adds turns and tool_calls get_run_stats Totals over a time window, or one row per day, user, source, or tool that errored; group_by takes several at once and reads the window once get_trajectory One run's ATIF trajectory, paged by step, long text clipped get_run_files, download_run_file Files the run produced find_experiments, get_experiments, get_experiment_runs Experiments, their scorecard, and per-case scores with evaluator explanations

Every tool answers {data, meta}, with data a list of rows. Search tools page with limit and offset (meta.next_offset is the next page); tools that take ids answer one row per id in input order, with note: {"code": "not_found"} for an unknown one. Dates are start_date / end_date (YYYY-MM-DD, inclusive, or an ISO 8601 timestamp). Money is {"value", "unit": "currency", "currency": "USD"}. Errors read <code>: <detail>. Tools that read trajectories have a time budget for the whole call, listing included: a run not read in time comes back as a row with error and detail instead of metrics, counted in meta.failed by get_runs; ask for it again with get_runs. Optional fields with no value are left out of rows. When listing alone uses the budget, the call fails with harness_timeout; narrow the window. With failed_only or tool_error, find_runs reads the window again on every call, so take one page and fetch the runs not read with get_runs rather than paging on.

A turn is one user message and everything the agent did until the next one. cost_source is reported when the harness priced the run, estimated when evalkit priced it from token counts, mixed for both. A turn counts as failed when the harness marks a step in it with extra.is_error (see Harness API).

user_id and client_id are what the harness recorded. Resolve them to people and firms with your identity service.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
From nothing to a scored experiment on an evalkit server your team already runs. Each step links to its full page; Concepts explains the terms.

No server yet? Try locally runs one on your machine with a sample agent and your own LLM, and ends with how to deploy one for your team.

docs.title: 1. Pick how evalkit reaches your agent
docs.text:
Path What you build Pick it when SDK run + traces A Python script that calls your agent once per case, and an OpenTelemetry exporter to this server The default: start here. Runs start from your machine or CI Harness API An HTTP service: start a run, report its status, serve its ATIF trajectory A deployed agent the server should drive (shared agents, runs started from the UI), or you need the Workspace tab Harness API + traces The same service minus the trajectory endpoint; the trajectory comes from your spans You want the Harness API but your agent already emits OpenTelemetry spans

The Workspace tab on a run lists the files the agent wrote. evalkit reads them through the Harness API files endpoints, so only the two Harness API paths have it. See Harness API for what each endpoint enables.

docs.title: 2. Install and log in
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.3.0"
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020

More in Install and Login.

docs.title: 3. Write evalkit.yaml and one case
docs.text:
At the root of the repository that holds your eval cases:

cases: eval/cases
fixtures: eval/fixtures

credentials:
  agents:
    myagent: env:MYAGENT_API_KEY # only for a Harness API agent that needs a key
  llm_providers:
    https://litellm.example.com: env:LITELLM_API_KEY # the server's judge base URL

Put the keys in a .env next to evalkit.yaml. Then create your agent on the server once:

# SDK path: a code-driven agent whose trajectory comes from its traces
evalkit agents create myagent --trajectory-source otel --mapping openinference.json
# Harness API path
evalkit agents create myagent --harness-url http://localhost:8080/evalkit/v1

openinference.json (or gen_ai.json) comes from the connect-traces skill.

Each directory under cases is a dataset. Add eval/cases/smoke/cases.yaml:

cases:
  - id: store-count
    input:
      question: "How many company-operated stores did Starbucks have at FY2021 year-end?"
    evaluators:
      output:
        answer_rubrics:
          rubrics:
            - rubric: "States 17,133 company-operated stores at FY2021 year-end."
              type: factual_retrieval

More in Config.

docs.title: 4. Run it
docs.text:
SDK path: install the SDK into your project (see Install), then write eval/run.py:

from evalkit.sdk import run_experiment, tracing
from myagent import ask

tracing.register(agent="myagent")

def task(input: dict) -> str:
    return ask(input["question"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_experiment(dataset="smoke", agent="myagent", task=task, dry_run=True)

dry_run=True runs one case without creating an experiment and prints what the server made of the spans. When it looks right, drop dry_run; run_experiment then returns a result whose url is the experiment page. More in SDK runs and Tracing.

Harness API path:

evalkit harness check myagent    # exercises every capability the harness declares
evalkit run smoke --agent myagent

A run executes every case it selects, whether the dataset is in your own workspace (smoke) or a shared one (smoke@dev). Review state never filters a run.

docs.title: 5. Read the results
docs.text: evalkit run prints the scorecard when it finishes. On this server, open the dataset under Datasets and pick the experiment. The experiment page has the scorecard; each run opens its trajectory, scores and, on the Harness API paths, its workspace files. If converted spans look wrong (missing messages, wrong span kinds), check one session with evalkit traces check myagent <session id> and see Mappings.

docs.title: 6. Attach a file to a case
docs.text:
Drop the file in the fixtures directory from your evalkit.yaml, register it once in fixtures.yaml at the root of your cases directory, and name it in the case. The context line is what the agent is told about the file.

cp ~/Downloads/meridian-balance-sheet.csv <fixtures>/
shasum -a 256 <fixtures>/meridian-balance-sheet.csv       # sha256 for the registry

# <cases>/fixtures.yaml
fixtures:
  - key: meridian-balance-sheet.csv
    sha256: 652d32…eece7
    context: Meridian's FY2025 balance sheet, USD thousands.

# in the case
- id: net-debt-fy2025
  fixtures: [meridian-balance-sheet.csv]
  input:
    question: Using only the attached file, what was net debt at FY2025 year-end?

A run or sync uploads any fixture whose sha256 the server doesn't hold yet, and the server keeps one copy per sha256. So you only need the files you touch, and if the bytes on disk don't match the registry the run stops and shows both hashes.

docs.title: 7. Iterate and promote
docs.text:
evalkit evaluate <experiment-id>        # re-score the same runs after an evaluator change; no agent calls
evalkit runs pull --experiment <experiment-id>   # download every run (trajectory, case, scores) to diagnose failures

Cases reach a shared dataset through a PR. On merge, CI syncs them into a shared workspace such as dev, where they start Unreviewed; a reviewer of that workspace approves them, and if dev is linked to prod, approval promotes them there.

evalkit review request finance@dev --case-id net-debt-fy2025 --reviewer <user>
evalkit review approve finance@dev net-debt-fy2025   # reviewers only

If an admin linked dev to a promotion target (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod), that approval also lands the case in finance@prod, approved. prod takes cases only that way: no sync, no separate review. The case page in either workspace shows the other's version and links to it.

docs.title: SDK runs
docs.text:
run_experiment runs an experiment from your own code: it calls your task once per case and repetition, stores the runs on this server, and scores them with the judge, the remote evaluators of the agent's workspace and any Python evaluators you pass. The agent is a code-driven agent on the server (no harness URL), created once with evalkit agents create. Invoking the agent, timeouts and stopping are your code.

# eval/run.py — uv run python eval/run.py
from evalkit.sdk import run_experiment, RunResult, evaluator, tracing
from myagent import MyAgent, setup_tracing

setup_tracing()                          # your own OpenTelemetry provider and instrumentors
tracing.register(agent="myagent-sdk")   # add this server as an export destination
agent = MyAgent()

def task(input: dict, files: list) -> str:
    return agent.ask(input["question"], attachments=[f.path for f in files])

@evaluator(name="citation_check")
def citation_check(case, run) -> float:
    cited = {c["url"] for c in (run.output or {}).get("citations", [])}
    return 1.0 if cited >= set(case.config["required"]) else 0.0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task,
                            evaluators=[citation_check], concurrency=4)
    print(result.url)

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
A sync or async callable. Parameters bind by name from this set, so their order does not matter; any other required parameter is an error before the first call, and an optional one keeps its default.

Parameter Value input the case input, verbatim, minus files files list[Fixture], the case's fixture files, downloaded before the call model the model argument of run_experiment, or None metadata a dict with the keys below

A Fixture has:

  • name: the fixture key the case names.
  • path: where the file sits on this machine.
  • context: the file's description from the fixture registry, or None. A Harness API agent gets the same text with each file; show it to your agent the same way (for example an "Attached files" block ahead of the question).

metadata holds:

  • session_id: the SDK's session id for this run, the session.id of its evalkit.run span.
  • experiment_id: the experiment, or None on a dry run.
  • case_id: the case.
  • repetition: 1 for the first repetition, 2 for the second, and so on.
  • tags: the case's tags.

model is the only way run_experiment(model=...) reaches your agent. The experiment records the requested model either way, so a task without a model parameter would silently run the agent's default; run_experiment prints a warning before the first call when that happens.

A task with exactly one parameter whose name is not in the table (def task(q)) receives the input. Return a str (the answer), a dict (the structured output) or a RunResult:

from evalkit.sdk import RunResult

RunResult(answer="…", output={"citations": []}, model="gpt-5",
          session_id="…",          # override the session the SDK polls
          trajectory={...})        # push an ATIF document instead of tracing

A task that raises records the run as failed with the exception and the experiment continues.

docs.title: An agent in another process
docs.text:
The SDK stamps session.id and the evalkit.* attributes only on spans made in this Python process. An agent behind HTTP or a job queue, or written in another language, joins the run in one of two ways. Pick one, not both.

  • Continue the trace. Inject the W3C trace context into the request and have the agent start its spans from it. Every span in a trace belongs to the session of the trace's root, the SDK's evalkit.run span, even if the agent stamps its own session.id or gen_ai.conversation.id.
from opentelemetry import propagate

def task(input: dict) -> str:
    headers: dict[str, str] = {}
    propagate.inject(headers)            # adds traceparent
    return httpx.post(AGENT_URL, json=input, headers=headers).json()["answer"]
  • Return the agent's session. The agent puts its own session id on its root span as session.id, and the task returns it. Use this when the trace context cannot reach the agent, for example through a queue. The SDK moves its evalkit.run span into that session, so no empty session is left behind, and the trajectory is built from the agent's trace.
def task(input: dict) -> RunResult:
    job = agent_api.start(input["question"])           # your API returns the session it opened
    return RunResult(answer=job.wait(), session_id=job.session_id)

If your API cannot tell you the session id, send it one instead: pass metadata["session_id"] along with the job and have the agent use it as its session id (or wrap the job in tracing.eval_run(metadata), see Tracing). Its spans then join the SDK's session and the task returns only the answer.

def task(input: dict, metadata: dict) -> str:
    return queue.submit(input["question"], session_id=metadata["session_id"]).wait()

Either way the Runs page links the session to its experiment and case.

The agent's exporter needs its own token. Mint one with evalkit tokens create --agent <name>; it never expires. Your login token expires, and an exporter that holds it then drops every span with nothing but a line in its own log.

docs.title: Datasets and workspaces
docs.text:
• dataset="finance" runs your own workspace's copy; if finance is a directory under cases it is synced first.
  • dataset="finance@dev" or dataset="finance", workspace="dev" runs the shared cases, every review state included.
  • case_ids=[...], split="...", repetitions, model and resume=<experiment id> mean what the same options mean on evalkit run.
  • dry_run=True runs one case (dry_run=N runs N) without creating an experiment and prints the answer and what the server made of the session. If the server cannot read a session, that case prints a trajectory read failed line and the dry run goes on. Use it while wiring up tracing; the session shows on the Runs page with its case question and case id.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
run_experiment refuses to run inside a running event loop. In a notebook use the async form:

from evalkit.sdk import arun_experiment

result = await arun_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task)

docs.title: The agent and the judge
docs.text:
agent="myagent-sdk" names an agent on the server; a bare name means your own workspace. Create it once:

evalkit agents create myagent-sdk --trajectory-source otel --mapping openinference.json \
  --max-concurrent-runs 4 --provides thinking=true

Its answer rule and exclude_spans live in its span mapping. evalkit.yaml is still required; it holds the cases, fixtures and credentials.

The judge is the server's default unless you pass one:

from evalkit.sdk import Judge, run_experiment

run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task,
               judge=Judge(base_url="https://litellm.example.com", model="gpt-5"))

An admin sets the default judge with evalkit judge-default set. Either way, the SDK reads the judge's key from credentials.llm_providers in evalkit.yaml, keyed by the judge's base URL.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: A code-driven agent has no GET /capabilities, so evalkit writes its capabilities onto each experiment itself: trajectory, tool_calls, token_usage and run_listing are true; thinking, artifacts and workspace are false. Evaluators gated on a capability skip when it is false. evalkit does not read capabilities from the spans. Set provides on the agent (evalkit agents create --provides, or evalkit agents edit) to declare what it really does, for example thinking: true when its spans carry the model's reasoning. Declare only what works: a false true produces failing scores blamed on the agent.

docs.title: Python evaluators
docs.text: @evaluator(name=..., kind="evaluator" | "gauge", requires_trajectory=False) turns a function into an evaluator. It receives the same EvalCase and EvalRun the HTTP Custom Evaluator API sends: the case id, input, expected block and this evaluator's config from the case YAML; the answer, structured output and the ATIF trajectory as a dict. Return a float, a ScoreItem, or a list of them. A case selects it by name under evaluators.custom, exactly like an HTTP evaluator.

docs.title: Bring your own benchmark
docs.text:
A published benchmark is a suite plus a Python evaluator:

  1. Write a script that turns the benchmark's file into case YAML. Each case gets the question as input. Its grading data (rubrics, reference answer) goes under evaluators.custom.<grader name>.
  2. evalkit sync <dir> puts it in a dataset like any suite.
  3. Write the grader as an @evaluator with that name. It reads the grading data from case.config, and calls its own judge models if it needs any. Pass it to run_experiment.

evalkit lint and evalkit sync warn with W-CUSTOM-UNKNOWN for the grader name, because the server can't see a Python evaluator. That warning is expected.

docs.title: Re-scoring
docs.text:
Python evaluators live in your script, so a re-score that needs them starts from the script:

from evalkit.sdk import evaluate_experiment

evaluate_experiment(experiment_id="…", evaluators=[citation_check],
                    refetch_trajectories=True)

refetch_trajectories polls the collector again for runs whose trajectory was partial or unavailable and re-scores them. evalkit evaluate refuses experiments that used Python evaluators and points here.

Next: Tracing.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
The collector is an OTLP/HTTP endpoint on this server:

POST http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces

It accepts application/x-protobuf and application/json, gzip or not, from any OpenTelemetry SDK. Spans are stored as received and converted to ATIF with the agent's mapping when a run or the Runs page asks for them.

docs.title: From Python with the SDK
docs.text:
from evalkit.sdk import tracing

tracing.register(agent="myagent-sdk")

register adds an exporter for this server to your global tracer provider, creating one if none is set. Your existing exporters keep running. The exporter carries an X-Evalkit-Agent header, which names the agent on the server; the evalkit.agent resource attribute is only set when register creates the provider itself. It reads the server URL from EVALKIT_SERVER_URL or your evalkit login, and the token from EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN (an agent token), then EVALKIT_TOKEN, then your evalkit login. It needs the otel extra.

docs.title: An existing span pipeline
docs.text:
register changes the global provider. When you build your own pipeline, take evalkit's parts and put them where you need them:

from evalkit.sdk import tracing

exporter = tracing.exporter(agent="myagent-sdk")    # OTLPSpanExporter: URL, token and X-Evalkit-Agent set
processor = tracing.processor(agent="myagent-sdk")  # batch processor around that exporter
provider.add_span_processor(processor)              # what register does for you
headers = tracing.headers(agent="myagent-sdk")      # the same headers, for an exporter you build yourself

All three resolve the server and token the same way register does. processor also stamps the run's session.id and evalkit.* attributes on spans that start under a task call (or under tracing.eval_run, below).

Spans handed straight to a processor or exporter, for example by a bridge that converts another tool's spans, never pass through the provider, so register cannot see them. Hand them to tracing.processor(...) too: give the bridge that processor, or one processor that fans out to all of yours and evalkit's (OpenTelemetry's SynchronousMultiSpanProcessor). Those spans are already finished, so processor cannot stamp them: the bridge copies session.id onto each span it converts. How eval-only export treats them is below.

docs.title: Choosing what a shared worker exports
docs.text:
A worker that serves both app runs (production, staging or manual use) and eval runs exports every span it makes, so every app turn also becomes a session on this server, which you can browse on the Runs page and pull with evalkit runs pull <agent> --source app. Whether to send app traffic is your choice. eval_run marks eval runs either way, and to send only those, filter on the mark:

from evalkit.sdk import tracing

provider.add_span_processor(tracing.processor(agent="myagent", only=tracing.is_eval_span))

def handle_job(job):
    if job.evalkit:                           # the task's metadata, sent along with the job
        with tracing.eval_run(job.evalkit):
            return run_agent(job)
    return run_agent(job)

The task passes its metadata argument along with the job (see SDK runs). eval_run stamps session.id (the SDK's session id), evalkit.case_id, evalkit.experiment_id and evalkit.repetition on every span started inside it, so the worker's spans join the run's session and the task returns only the answer. is_eval_span is true for a span that carries evalkit.case_id. The stamp lives in a context variable: spans started in another thread need that thread to run inside eval_run too.

A harness agent learns that a run is an eval run from the metadata of POST /runs: experiment_id, case_id and repetition. That is what it passes to eval_run, with the run_id it returns as the session id: tracing.eval_run({**metadata, "session_id": run_id}).

only decides by trace, not by span. It is any function that takes a span and returns a bool, and it runs on each span as the span starts and again as it ends. Once it is true for one span, the processor keeps every span of that span's trace that reaches it: spans started inside eval_run, the job's own spans started before eval_run in the same trace, and finished spans a bridge hands straight to the processor. Spans of other traces are dropped. A custom only picks whole traces the same way.

The rule for order: a span is kept when its trace is already marked by the time the span ends. The first span started inside eval_run marks its trace as it starts, before anything under it ends, so spans that end before it and spans a bridge hands over later are both kept. A span that ends before any span of its trace was marked is dropped. A bridge that may hand spans over that early can copy the evalkit.* attributes onto them, so each one marks its own trace. A bridge should copy session.id either way: the server takes a trace's session from its root span when the root reaches it, and from each span's own session.id otherwise.

The processor remembers the 10,000 most recently used eval traces and forgets the oldest. Each kept span refreshes its trace, so a trace is only forgotten once 10,000 other eval traces have been used since its last span.

Spans from another process in the same trace, such as an MCP gateway pod the agent calls, never reach this processor. They go through that process's own exporter, so that process makes its own choice: either it continues the trace, wraps its work in eval_run with the run's metadata sent along with the request, and filters with only=tracing.is_eval_span too, or it exports everything.

Do not use a sampler for this: a sampler drops spans for every exporter, your own backend included.

Around every task call the SDK opens a root span named evalkit.run with session.id set to the run id, and stamps session.id, evalkit.experiment_id, evalkit.case_id and evalkit.repetition onto every span your code starts underneath it. That is what groups a trace into one session. When the task returns RunResult(session_id=...), the root span takes that session id instead, so it joins the agent's session rather than sitting alone; see SDK runs for agents in another process.

docs.title: From any OpenTelemetry SDK
docs.text:
Point the exporter at the collector and name the agent, either with a header or an attribute:

export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer <token>,X-Evalkit-Agent=myagent"
export OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="evalkit.agent=myagent"   # alternative to the header

The collector picks the agent per span: the span's evalkit.agent attribute first, then the resource's, then the X-Evalkit-Agent header. One process that serves several agents can therefore share one exporter and set evalkit.agent on each agent's spans. The value is an agent reference (myagent or myagent@workspace). Every agent a batch names is checked as if it came in the header: an agent token writes only its own agent, a login token only agents in workspaces you can write to (your own, or a shared one where you are a writer). If any span names an agent the token may not write, the whole batch is refused.

Put the session id on the root span of each trace, in the attribute your mapping's session_id rule names (session.id in openinference.json, gen_ai.conversation.id in gen_ai.json). Every span in a trace belongs to the session of the trace's root, even one that carries a session attribute of its own. Only when the root has no session do child spans keep theirs.

docs.title: Deployed agents
docs.text:
A service cannot carry a person's token. Mint an agent token, bound to one agent and valid only for the collector:

evalkit tokens create --agent ouragent@dev     # needs writer on dev
evalkit tokens list
evalkit tokens revoke <id>

Set it on the deployment as EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN next to EVALKIT_SERVER_URL; tracing.register, tracing.exporter and tracing.processor pick both up. For a non-Python exporter put it in OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS. Use an agent token for any exporter outside the process that calls run_experiment too, even on your laptop: the login token expires under a long-running worker.

The collector logs every refused export as otel export rejected with the status, the reason (expired token, invalid token, unknown agent, forbidden, too large, malformed) and the agent. OpenTelemetry exporters only log a failed export on their side, so a silent agent is worth checking in both logs.

docs.title: Size limits and large spans
docs.text:
LLM spans from OpenInference and GenAI instrumentations carry the full input of each call: the messages so far, the system prompt and the tool schemas. Every turn repeats the whole context, so a long agent session grows with roughly the square of its turns. A 14-minute chat with subagents can store hundreds of MB of span attributes.

The server has two limits, both set in its config:

Limit Default What happens past it otel.max_batch_bytes 16 MiB One export request (after gzip is undone) gets 413 and its spans are dropped. Exporters do not split a refused batch, so keep batches small. otel.max_session_bytes 384 MiB Reading the session (a run's trajectory, evalkit traces check, the Mappings tab) gets 413 with the session's size and the limit. A run records the trajectory as unavailable and logs the message. --dump spans.json still works.

otel.max_session_bytes counts the span attributes a trajectory build loads, not everything stored. evalkit reads the input messages (and system prompt) of an LLM span only for the first LLM call of each agent and subagent; later calls add only their output, tool calls and tokens to the trajectory. So the build leaves the input of every later LLM call in the database and does not count it. The limit keeps one session from using up the server's memory, so raise it only together with the server's memory limit.

For agents with large spans, send fewer spans per export and give each export more time. For the Python SDK, tracing.register included:

export OTEL_BSP_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE=16   # spans per export; default 512
export OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE=2048        # spans waiting for export; raise it if the exporter logs "Queue full"
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT=60       # seconds per export in Python; default 10

Other SDKs follow the OpenTelemetry spec and read OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT in milliseconds (60000). A 10 MB span can take more than 10 s to upload, longer than the default timeout. In an OpenTelemetry Collector, set send_batch_max_size on the batch processor and timeout on the otlphttp exporter instead.

docs.title: Exporting to evalkit and another backend
docs.text:
The standard OTLP variables name one endpoint. To keep exporting to your tracing backend and send the same spans here, either:

  • add a second otlphttp exporter to the OpenTelemetry Collector the agent already exports to (recommended for deployed agents), or
  • add a second span processor and exporter in code. tracing.register does this for Python.
exporters:
  otlphttp/evalkit:
    traces_endpoint: http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${env:EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN}
      X-Evalkit-Agent: ouragent@dev
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      exporters: [otlp/existing, otlphttp/evalkit]

The collector speaks OTLP over HTTP only, not gRPC. Bodies may be chunked with no Content-Length (the JavaScript exporter sends them that way); a proxy in front of the collector must allow that.

docs.title: The main agent and subagents
docs.text: Mark the agent's top-level span as an AGENT span (openinference.span.kind=AGENT, or gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent). evalkit builds the main trajectory from it, and every AGENT span inside it becomes a subagent trajectory named by the span's agent.name (gen_ai.agent.name), or by the span name when that is missing. When the root span is not an AGENT span, as with the SDK's evalkit.run span, evalkit takes the earliest AGENT span that is not inside another one as the main agent. If that span is a tool call that starts a subagent partway through the run, the subagent's steps land in the main trajectory and the call has no result, so mark the top-level span as an AGENT span rather than relying on this.

docs.title: Harness agents with traces
docs.text:
A harness agent created with --trajectory-source otel keeps the whole Harness API flow and skips GET /runs/{id}/trajectory: it puts the run id it returned on its spans, in the attribute its mapping's session_id rule names, and evalkit polls the session until it settles. The harness declares provides.trajectory: false; evalkit still runs the trajectory evaluators because the trajectory comes from the collector.

The session evalkit polls is the run_id that POST /runs returns, so there is no separate session field. A queue-backed agent whose worker picks its own session id returns that id as run_id, or puts the run_id it returned on its spans in that session attribute. To export only eval runs from a harness that also serves production, see Choosing what a shared worker exports above.

docs.title: Importing history from a trace source
docs.text:
An admin registers a trace source (a Phoenix server) once. After that, any user can import traces from it into an OTel agent they can write, with evalkit traces import or the agent page's Import tab.

  • The trace source's API key is shared with every user in effect: anyone can import any project that key can read.
  • Imported traces land in the agent's workspace. Every user can read every workspace, so traces imported into your personal workspace are visible to everyone on the server. See Where runs happen.

docs.title: Checking a session
docs.text:
evalkit traces check myagent-sdk <session id>

prints the settle state, span kinds, tokens, the attributes the mapping did not read and the ATIF summary. --dump spans.json writes the raw spans. --dump esf.json leaves out the input messages of every LLM call after each agent's first, as the trajectory does not use them; spans.json has the raw values. A session over otel.max_session_bytes fails the check with its size and the limit (see Size limits and large spans above). If the kinds or messages look wrong, the agent needs a mapping: see Mappings.

docs.title: Try evalkit locally
docs.text:
The try-it stack runs evalkit on your machine and walks you through the default way to connect an agent: an SDK run with OpenTelemetry traces. Your Python code calls the agent once per case. The agent's spans go to evalkit, evalkit turns them into a trajectory, and your LLM judges the answers. The kit includes a small sample agent that calls your LLM, so you get a real scorecard before you touch your own agent.

It is not a deployment: it uses a demo admin password and keeps everything on one machine. For a real deployment, follow the evalkit-deployment skill.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• uv and port 8020 free.
  • An OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint (OpenAI, a LiteLLM proxy, vLLM, Ollama, ...) that supports tool calls and structured output, with its base URL, API key and model name. The sample agent and the judge both use it.
  • Either Postgres 15 or newer running on this machine (without Docker), or Docker with Compose v2 (with Docker).

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text: Pick one way. Both end with the server on http://localhost:8020 and the try kit in a folder, and the steps after this section are the same.

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text:
evalkit is on PyPI as evalkit-py. Install it with the server extra, then let evalkit init-server set up the rest:

uv tool install "evalkit-py[server]"   # or: pip install "evalkit-py[server]"
evalkit init-server
cd evalkit-try
evalkit serve

init-server asks for the Postgres URL (default postgresql+psycopg://localhost/evalkit), your LLM's base URL, model and API key, and the admin password (default evalkit-admin). A question is skipped when its flag or environment variable is set (evalkit init-server --help lists both); --yes never asks. It then:

  • creates the database when it does not exist, and migrates it
  • registers your LLM as the LLM provider try and makes it the default judge, with its API key stored encrypted in the database
  • copies the try kit into ./evalkit-try
  • writes config.yaml there, with blobs stored under evalkit-try/data
  • writes .env beside it, with your LLM settings, the admin password and the key that encrypts stored API keys; evalkit serve reads it. Keep .env: without that key the server cannot read the stored LLM key

Leave evalkit serve running and use another terminal for the steps below, from the evalkit-try folder. The CLI is already installed, so skip the install command in step 1.

docs.title: With Docker
docs.text:
The kit is skills/evalkit-deployment/try/ in the evalkit repository, and the server image holds a copy. The first --build takes a few minutes (it builds the web UI and installs the server); later starts take seconds.

From an evalkit checkout, compose builds the image:

cd skills/evalkit-deployment/try
cp -n .env.example .env          # fill in LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL
docker compose up -d --wait --build

With the server image instead, copy the kit out of it first:

export EVALKIT_IMAGE=<registry>/evalkit:<tag>
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD:/out" "$EVALKIT_IMAGE" \
  evalkit init-server --kit-only --dir /out/evalkit-try
cd evalkit-try
cp -n .env.example .env          # fill in LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL
docker compose up -d --wait

Compose starts Postgres and the evalkit server, with your LLM as the judge. --wait returns once the server is healthy. The server runs migrations on every start.

docs.title: What's in the kit
docs.text: File What it is agent.py The sample agent. It answers questions about Acme Widgets, a made-up company, by calling your LLM with one tool, lookup_financials. It records each model call and tool call as an OpenTelemetry span, using the GenAI semantic conventions. run.py The SDK run: tracing.register sends the spans to evalkit, and run_experiment calls the agent once per case and scores the answers. mapping.json The span mapping: which span attribute holds the model, the messages, the tokens and each tool call. It starts as the connect-traces skill's gen_ai.json. cases/acme/ Five cases in two folders (tags), with answer rubrics and a tool check. evalkit.yaml, .env Where the cases are, and the judge's key. config.yaml The server's config. docker-compose.yml, .env.example With Docker only: the stack, and the template for its .env. init-server leaves them out.

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI and log in
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.3.0"   # with Docker only
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020 --username admin --password evalkit-admin

0.3.0 is the server's version; curl http://localhost:8020/api/cli prints it.

evalkit login replaces any login you already saved. To keep it, skip evalkit login and point this shell at the try-it server instead (this needs jq):

export EVALKIT_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:8020
export EVALKIT_TOKEN=$(curl -fsSL -X POST http://localhost:8020/api/auth/login \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"username": "admin", "password": "evalkit-admin"}' | jq -r .token)

run.py declares its own dependencies at the top of the file, so uv run run.py installs what it needs on the first run. The kit pins evalkit to the server's version when evalkit init-server copies it. In an evalkit checkout, run the kit's scripts with the checkout instead: uv run --project ../../.. --extra otel python run.py.

docs.title: 2. Connect the agent's traces
docs.text:
Create the agent. Its trajectories come from its spans, read with mapping.json:

evalkit agents create analyst --trajectory-source otel --mapping mapping.json

Run one case without creating an experiment:

uv run run.py --dry-run

It prints the answer, the session id with a count of its spans by kind and the mapping version, and whether evalkit built a valid trajectory from them. If no spans arrived, check that run.py calls tracing.register before the agent runs.

Then see how the mapping read that session:

evalkit traces check analyst <session id>

It prints one line per check: the session settled, the root span, the mapping version, the model calls and their token totals, the tool calls matched to the model's calls, any span attribute the mapping does not read, and a summary of the trajectory. Every line should have a ✓.

docs.title: 3. First scorecard
docs.text:
uv run run.py

run_experiment syncs cases/acme into your own workspace (acme@admin), runs the five cases, has your LLM judge each answer against its rubrics, checks that the agent called lookup_financials, and prints the scorecard and the experiment URL. The scores depend on your model. acme-operating-margin asks for a figure the agent has no data for, so it passes only if the agent says so instead of making one up.

The answer_rubric_* rows by rubric type (factual_retrieval, derived_computation, analysis_interpretation) count only the cases that have a rubric of that type, so their case counts differ.

Open http://localhost:8020, log in as admin with the admin password, and open the experiment under the acme dataset. Each run shows its trajectory, the judge's verdict on every rubric and the tool check. The Runs page lists the raw sessions.

docs.title: 4. Iterate
docs.text:
This is the loop you will run on your own agent:

  • Change the agent, for example the instructions in agent.py, and run run.py again. Compare the two experiments in the UI.
  • Edit or add a case under cases/acme/ and run again. The run syncs the folder first.
  • Run one folder: run_experiment(..., split="balance-sheet").

docs.title: 5. Connect your own agent
docs.text:
Do the same in your own repository:

  1. Traces. If your agent already emits OpenTelemetry spans (OpenInference or GenAI conventions), keep them. If not, add an instrumentor for your LLM library, for example openinference-instrumentation-openai for the OpenAI client (OpenInference publishes one per popular library), or record GenAI spans yourself as this kit's agent.py does (Tracing). The connect-traces skill writes or checks the span mapping (Mappings).
  2. Setup. Put an evalkit.yaml at the root of your repository, with cases: pointing at your cases directory and the judge's key under credentials.llm_providers. That map is keyed by the judge's base URL, which must match the judge the run uses: the server's default judge (http://localhost:8020/api/judge-default shows its base_url), or the one you pass to run_experiment(judge=...). This kit keys it with env:LLM_BASE_URL so the URL comes from .env. Keep the keys in a .env beside evalkit.yaml.
  3. Script. Copy run.py. Pin evalkit in its header to your evalkit server's version (evalkit-py[otel]==<version>), call tracing.register(agent="myagent"), and write a task that calls your agent with the case input. uv run run.py builds an environment from the header alone, so add your agent's packages to its dependencies. If your agent lives in a uv project, you can instead add evalkit to the project (see the Install page) and run the script with uv run python run.py.
  4. Cases. Add a folder under your cases directory, for example mine/, and run with dataset="mine". The authoring-eval-cases skill covers the format. See Concepts for the terms.
  5. Agent and mapping. Copy this kit's mapping.json into your repository, or openinference.json from the connect-traces skill if your spans follow OpenInference, and create the agent with it: evalkit agents create myagent --trajectory-source otel --mapping my-mapping.json. Do a dry run with your script and evalkit traces check on its session, as in step 2. For each ! line, edit your copy, upload it as a draft and preview the same session:
evalkit traces mapping push myagent my-mapping.json
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --mapping draft

When it reads right, activate it: evalkit traces mapping push myagent my-mapping.json --activate, or use the agent's Mappings tab in the web UI. Runs always use the active mapping. The connect-traces skill walks a coding agent through the same loop.

SDK runs covers the rest: agents in another process, Python evaluators, and re-scoring. If the evalkit server should drive your agent instead of your script (runs started from the UI, shared agents), implement the Harness API.

docs.title: Next: run evalkit for your team
docs.text: The try-it stack is for one machine. For a server your team shares, follow the evalkit-deployment skill: it covers the server image, Postgres, blob storage, the judge, migrations and the first users and workspaces. A coding agent can walk it with you. Once the server runs, your teammates start from its own /docs page.

docs.title: Stop and clean up
docs.text:
Without Docker: stop evalkit serve with Ctrl-C. To delete everything, drop the database you gave init-server (dropdb evalkit with the default URL) and remove the evalkit-try folder.

With Docker:

docker compose down        # stop; data stays in the volumes
docker compose down -v     # stop and delete all data

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text:
• uv run run.py cannot find evalkit-py==<version>: that version is not on PyPI yet (a source build, or a build whose publish job has not finished). Run it with the wheel you installed instead: uv run --no-project --with "<path to the wheel>[otel]" python run.py, or from an evalkit checkout: uv run --project <checkout> --extra otel python run.py. Or wait for the publish.
  • init-server cannot connect: start Postgres (brew services start postgresql@17, sudo systemctl start postgresql, or Postgres.app), or pass --database-url with the user and password your Postgres needs, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://me:secret@localhost:5432/evalkit.
  • init-server says config.yaml exists: you already set up that folder. Run evalkit serve there, or pass --force to write it again.
  • evalkit serve says a variable is not set: check .env beside config.yaml.
  • Compose says a variable is not set: fill in .env (copied from .env.example).
  • Compose cannot find evalkit:try: outside a checkout, set EVALKIT_IMAGE; in a checkout, add --build.
  • The server will not start: docker compose logs server (and check that .env is filled in: the server reads the LLM settings at start).
  • The server exits with code 132 and no logs (Apple Silicon): the image is older than 0.22.0. Add OPENSSL_armcap: "0" to the server's environment: in docker-compose.yml, or use a newer image.
  • The judge fails on every case: your endpoint must support structured output (response_format with a JSON schema). Try another model.
  • evalkit or run.py talks to another server: run the evalkit login above again, or check EVALKIT_SERVER_URL.

docs.title: Where runs happen
docs.text:
Every dataset and agent lives in a workspace:

  • Personal workspace: one per user, named after the username. Only the owner writes to it.
  • Shared workspace: created by an admin, e.g. dev and prod. Members with the writer role write to it; reviewers approve its cases.
  • Who can read: every logged-in user can read every workspace, including other users' personal workspaces: datasets, cases, experiments, runs, trajectories, spans and sessions, and fixtures. Only the owner writes to a personal workspace; admins and writers write to a shared one. The web UI marks someone else's personal workspace "read-only".
  • Traces are visible too: traces you import or export into your personal workspace, such as production traces pulled for case mining, can be read by everyone on the server. No workspace setting keeps them private. If traces hold data some users must not see, scrub it in your agent before export, or run a separate evalkit server for those traces. A mapping's exclude_spans does not help here: the server stores spans as received and only skips them when it builds a trajectory.
  • Promotion: an admin can link two shared workspaces (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod). Approving a case in finance@dev then adds that version to finance@prod, approved, with its overlays. prod is fed only by promotion: sync and review decisions there are refused, comments allowed. Create each target dataset once with evalkit datasets create finance@prod. One target per source, one source per target.

The agent you pick decides who drives the run. The dataset and the agent together decide where the experiment is stored:

  • Both shared: the experiment lives in the dataset's workspace.
  • Otherwise: it lives in your personal workspace.

Example with workspaces @alice (personal), @dev and @prod (shared). myagent is alice's personal agent; ouragent is the team's deployed agent, with one entry per shared workspace.

# Who / entry Dataset Agent Driver Agent runs on Trajectory from Experiment in Use case 1 alice, SDK run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent") finance@alice myagent@alice (code-driven) alice's Python laptop, in-process OTel → collector → server builds ATIF @alice EDD inner loop (default) 2 alice, evalkit run finance --agent myagent finance@alice myagent@alice (localhost harness) alice's CLI laptop harness ATIF → CLI → server @alice a Harness API agent on this machine 3 alice, evalkit run finance@prod --agent myagent finance@prod (approved only) myagent@alice alice's CLI laptop harness ATIF → CLI → server @alice does a local change break the released set 4 alice, evalkit run finance --agent ouragent@dev finance@alice ouragent@dev server dev cluster harness ATIF or OTel @alice try new cases on the deployed dev agent 5 anyone, UI or run finance@dev --agent ouragent@dev finance@dev ouragent@dev server dev cluster harness ATIF or OTel @dev regression after a deploy or merge 6 anyone, run finance@dev --agent ouragent@prod finance@dev ouragent@prod server prod cluster harness ATIF or OTel @dev does prod pass cases approved in dev 7 anyone, UI or run finance@prod --agent ouragent@prod finance@prod ouragent@prod server prod cluster harness ATIF or OTel @prod release gate 8 deployed ouragent with an agent token none ouragent@prod none prod cluster OTel → collector, browsed in Runs none trajectory debugging of deployed traffic (optional) ✗ anyone, server or UI, --agent myagent@alice any myagent@alice refused the server cannot reach a laptop ✗ bob, --agent myagent@alice any myagent@alice refused only the owner runs a personal agent

docs.title: Several branches
docs.text:
• evalkit run syncs the dataset directory first. The dataset in your workspace then matches whichever branch ran last, and the dataset page shows that sync's branch and sha.
  • An experiment pins its case versions when it starts. A sync from another branch never changes a running or finished experiment. Cases removed by that sync are soft-removed, and pinned versions remain.
  • Fixture bytes are content-addressed, so two branches never overwrite each other's bytes under the same key.
  • --resume does not sync, and runs the pinned versions, so it is safe from any branch.
  • Agent config is one row per agent, not per branch.

docs.title: SDK reference
docs.text: The Python SDK runs experiments from your own code. Install it with the otel extra at your server's version (see Install) and import from evalkit.sdk. SDK runs walks through it.

docs.title: run_experiment
docs.text:
run_experiment(
    *,
    dataset: str,
    agent: str,
    task: Task,
    workspace: str | None = None,
    evaluators: Sequence[PythonEvaluator] = (),
    repetitions: int = 1,
    concurrency: int | None = None,
    case_ids: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    split: str | None = None,
    model: str | None = None,
    resume: int | None = None,
    dry_run: bool | int = False,
    trajectory_wait_seconds: int | None = None,
    judge: JudgeSettings | None = None,
) -> ExperimentResult

Run an experiment: call task once per case and repetition, store the runs on the server and score them.

Scoring uses the judge, the remote evaluators of the agent's workspace and the Python evaluators you pass. Reads evalkit.yaml (cases, fixtures, credentials) from the current directory or a parent, and the login from evalkit login.

Parameters:

  • dataset (str) –

    The dataset to run. A bare name means your personal workspace; if it is also a directory under cases in evalkit.yaml, it is synced first. name@workspace runs a shared dataset, every review state included.

  • agent (str) –

    The code-driven agent on the server that the runs belong to, created once with evalkit agents create. A bare name means your personal workspace.

  • task (Task) –

    Your function, called once per case and repetition, sync or async. Its parameters bind by name from input (the case input), files (list[Fixture]), model and metadata (session_id, experiment_id, case_id, repetition, tags). A task with one parameter of another name receives the input. Return a str (the answer), a dict (the structured output) or a RunResult. A task that raises records a failed run.

  • workspace (str | None, default: None ) –

    The workspace of dataset when it is a bare name.

  • evaluators (Sequence[PythonEvaluator], default: () ) –

    Python evaluators made with evaluator. A case selects one by name under evaluators.custom, like an HTTP evaluator.

  • repetitions (int, default: 1 ) –

    How many times each case runs.

  • concurrency (int | None, default: None ) –

    How many tasks run at once. Defaults to the agent's max_concurrent_runs.

  • case_ids (Sequence[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Run only these cases.

  • split (str | None, default: None ) –

    Run only the cases of this split (a case tag).

  • model (str | None, default: None ) –

    Passed to the task's model parameter and recorded on the experiment.

  • resume (int | None, default: None ) –

    An experiment id to resume: runs only the cases it has not finished.

  • dry_run (bool | int, default: False ) –

    True runs one case without creating an experiment and prints the answer and what the server made of the session; an int runs that many.

  • trajectory_wait_seconds (int | None, default: None ) –

    How long to wait for a run's spans to settle into a trajectory. Defaults to the agent's setting.

  • judge (JudgeSettings | None, default: None ) –

    The judge for LLM-graded evaluators. Defaults to the server's default judge. Its API key comes from credentials.judges in evalkit.yaml, keyed by base_url.

Returns:

  • ExperimentResult –

    The experiment id, its URL and one summary per run.

Raises:

  • RuntimeError –

    When called from a running event loop; await arun_experiment there instead.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(
    agent: str, only: SpanFilter | None = None
) -> None

Send this process's OpenTelemetry spans to the evalkit server.

Adds an exporter to the global tracer provider, or creates one when none is set. Call it after your own tracing setup, so it joins your provider. Spans go to the server you logged in to (or EVALKIT_SERVER_URL), with your token or EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN (an agent token). Needs the otel extra.

Parameters:

docs.title: evaluator
docs.text:
evaluator(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> PythonEvaluator

evaluator(
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    kind: Kind = "evaluator",
    requires_trajectory: bool = False,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], PythonEvaluator]

evaluator(
    fn: Callable[..., Any] | None = None,
    /,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    kind: Kind = "evaluator",
    requires_trajectory: bool = False,
) -> (
    PythonEvaluator
    | Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], PythonEvaluator]
)

Turn a function into a Python evaluator for run_experiment.

Use it bare (@evaluator) or with options (@evaluator(name=...)). The function receives the same EvalCase and EvalRun the Custom Evaluator API sends: the case id, input, expected block and this evaluator's config from the case YAML (case.config); the answer, structured output and ATIF trajectory as a dict. It returns a float, a ScoreItem, or a list of them.

Parameters:

  • fn (Callable[..., Any] | None, default: None ) –

    The function, when used bare.

  • name (str | None, default: None ) –

    The name cases use under evaluators.custom. Defaults to the function's name.

  • kind (Kind, default: 'evaluator' ) –

    evaluator for a score, gauge for a measurement.

  • requires_trajectory (bool, default: False ) –

    Skip runs that have no trajectory.

Returns:

  • PythonEvaluator | Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], PythonEvaluator] –

    The evaluator, or a decorator that makes one.

docs.text:
What a task can return instead of a plain answer.

Attributes:

  • answer (str | None) –

    The agent's answer text.

  • output (dict[str, Any] | None) –

    The agent's structured output.

  • model (str | None) –

    The model the agent used, recorded on the run.

  • error (str | None) –

docs.text:
The LLM judge an experiment uses; exported from evalkit.sdk as Judge.

Its API key comes from credentials.judges in evalkit.yaml, keyed by base_url.

Attributes:

  • base_url (str) –

    An OpenAI-compatible endpoint that supports structured output.

  • model (str) –

    The model name at that endpoint.

  • reasoning_effort (str) –

    Passed to the model as reasoning_effort.

  • max_tokens (int) –

    The most tokens one judge reply may use.

  • concurrency (int) –
